input.strategy_title: Default Vector Store for Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag
input.strategy_markdown:
## Summary

RHOAI must provide a default vector store that is available out-of-the-box — without manual setup — so that Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag continue to function when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution image. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.

## Problem Statement

Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.

RHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.

Users expect vector storage to "just work" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.

## Affected Customers

* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities
* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag
* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store

## Business Justification

* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.
* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.
* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.

## Acceptance Criteria

* \[ \] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure
* \[ \] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)
* \[ \] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)
* \[ \] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead

## Success Criteria

* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution
* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience
* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation

## Open Questions

* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)
* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)

## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)

> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.

## Staff Engineer Input

**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that "every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.

**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS="$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.

**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.

**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.

**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.

**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.

**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.

**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.

**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.

**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.

**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. Remove any references to consolidating vector and application storage in a single database, and remove any SQLite-to-PostgreSQL upgrade path considerations.

# Operator-based PostgreSQL/pgvector provisioning for Gen AI Studio playground RAG

## Description

This epic delivers the default vector store for Gen AI Studio playground RAG using operator-based
self-provisioning, implemented in the RHOAI-controlled operator layer that the dashboard operator
modularization delivers. Following the model-registry-operator's auto-provisioning pattern, the
operator provisions a PostgreSQL instance with the pgvector extension for playgrounds with RAG
enabled, configures the OGXServer custom resource to use the remote pgvector vector_io provider, and
manages the instance lifecycle. This branch executes only if the go/no-go decision selects the
operator-based path (that is, the operator layer dependency lands in time for the target release).

## Scope

- Operator reconciliation logic that provisions the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance per the resolved
  scoping model: Deployment, Service, persistent storage, Secret with generated credentials, using
  the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image that already includes pgvector (no custom image build, no new
  pipeline onboarding; the image is already referenced for disconnected installs).
- Configuration of the OGXServer custom resource so the OGX instance uses the remote pgvector
  vector_io provider with connection details sourced from the provisioned Secret — the store runs as
  a separate process, decoupled from the OGX instance, and OGX application storage remains on its
  existing default (the vector_io provider configuration is independent of application storage).
- Lifecycle management in the operator: cleanup of the instance when its consuming playground is
  deleted, recovery after PostgreSQL pod restarts, and credential rotation.
- Resource requests/limits for the provisioned instance set per the pgvector benchmark's
  sizing recommendation (starting from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing).
- Portability design: the connection configuration is indirection-based so that when a
  platform-provided shared PostgreSQL becomes available in a future release, the operator can
  consume a shared connection string instead of self-provisioning.
- End-to-end validation of Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows against the provisioned default
  store (Gen AI Studio scope only; Auto Rag compatibility is handled in its own strategy).
- A disable/override path so users can configure an external vector database instead of the default.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Gen AI Studio playground with RAG enabled obtains a working default vector store with zero
  manual user configuration of external infrastructure.
- Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows (document ingest, retrieval, chat with RAG) function against
  the provisioned pgvector store with no loss of current capability.
- The vector store runs as a separate process from the OGX instance; no inline vector provider is
  used, and OGX application storage is unchanged.
- Multi-tenant scoping per the resolved scoping model is enforced and verifiable (for example,
  per-namespace isolation of vector data between tenants).
- The provisioned instance's resource requests/limits match the benchmark-informed sizing
  recommendation.
- Lifecycle is handled and demonstrable: the instance is cleaned up when its consuming playground is
  deleted, recovers after pod restarts, and credentials can be rotated without manual intervention.
- The PostgreSQL image used is the existing Red Hat image with pgvector included; no custom image
  build or new build-pipeline onboarding is introduced.
- The connection configuration can be repointed at a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL connection
  string without rearchitecting the provisioning (portability verified by design review or
  configuration test).
- Disabling the default provisioning and configuring an external vector database instead is
  supported and documented.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-1 (P0) — default vector store out-of-the-box:** this epic is the operator-based delivery of
  that capability.
- **HLR-2 (P0) — playground RAG with no loss of current capability:** covered by the end-to-end
  validation acceptance criteria (Gen AI Studio only; Auto Rag decoupled per Staff input).
- **HLR-3 (P0) — separate-process, non-inline vector store:** delivered via the remote pgvector
  vector_io provider configuration on the OGXServer custom resource.
- **HLR-4 (P1) — multi-tenant scoping (bundled):** implements the scoping model resolved by the
  scoping investigation; enforcing it is the same provisioning code and resource surface as HLR-1, so
  it is not split into a separate epic.
- **HLR-5 (P1) — lightweight/overhead (bundled):** applies the benchmark-informed resource sizing to
  the same provisioned Deployment spec; not separately schedulable.
- **HLR-6 (P2) — portability to a platform-shared database (bundled):** the connection-string
  indirection is a design constraint on the same configuration code; no independent user value.

## Risks / Notes

- **Failure impact of the scoping-model gate.** This epic also depends on the scoping-model
  investigation (its other direct dependency); if that investigation fails to ratify a scoping model,
  the provisioning topology this epic builds cannot be finalized — the gate's action is a rewrite of
  the topology. Mitigation: proceed on per-namespace scoping (the Gen AI Studio lead's stated
  preference) as an explicitly recorded working assumption, keep the scope selector parameterized in
  the provisioning logic so the ratified model can be adopted without rearchitecting, and re-escalate
  ratification in sprint planning. The `gate_failure_impact` frontmatter field records only the
  provisioning-approach go/no-go gate because the field is single-valued and that gate selects whether
  this branch epic exists at all; the failure impact above covers the scoping gate.

# BFF-managed PostgreSQL/pgvector provisioning for Gen AI Studio playground RAG

## Description

This epic delivers the default vector store for Gen AI Studio playground RAG using BFF-managed
provisioning: the gen-ai backend-for-frontend provisions the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly —
creating the Deployment, Service, persistent storage, and Secret when a playground with RAG is
configured and no suitable instance exists in the namespace — mirroring how the BFF already
provisions guardrails infrastructure. This branch executes only if the go/no-go decision selects the
fallback path (that is, the RHOAI-controlled operator layer from the dashboard operator modularization
does not land in time for the target release). Because the BFF is not an operator with a
reconciliation loop, lifecycle management (cleanup, restart recovery, credential rotation) receives
explicit design attention.

## Scope

- BFF provisioning logic that creates the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance per the resolved scoping model
  when a playground with RAG is configured and no suitable instance exists in the namespace
  (create-if-missing, reusing an existing instance when present): Deployment, Service, persistent
  storage claim, and Secret with generated credentials, using the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image
  that already includes pgvector (no custom image build, no new pipeline onboarding).
- Configuration of the OGXServer custom resource so the OGX instance uses the remote pgvector
  vector_io provider with connection details sourced from the provisioned Secret — the store runs as
  a separate process, decoupled from the OGX instance, and OGX application storage remains on its
  existing default (the vector_io provider configuration is independent of application storage).
- Lifecycle design and handling given the BFF has no reconciliation loop: cleanup of the instance when
  its consuming playground is deleted, recovery after PostgreSQL pod restarts, and credential
  rotation.
- Resource requests/limits for the provisioned instance set per the pgvector benchmark's sizing
  recommendation (starting from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing).
- Portability design: the BFF consumes an injected connection string rather than hardcoding
  self-provisioning, so that when a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL becomes available in a future
  release, the BFF can consume the shared connection string instead of self-provisioning.
- End-to-end validation of Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows against the provisioned default
  store (Gen AI Studio scope only; Auto Rag compatibility is handled in its own strategy).
- A disable/override path so users can configure an external vector database instead of the default.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Gen AI Studio playground with RAG enabled obtains a working default vector store with zero
  manual user configuration of external infrastructure.
- Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows (document ingest, retrieval, chat with RAG) function against

  used, and OGX application storage is unchanged.
- Provisioning is idempotent: when a suitable instance already exists in the namespace per the
  resolved scoping model, it is reused rather than duplicated.
- Multi-tenant scoping per the resolved scoping model is enforced and verifiable (for example,
  per-namespace isolation of vector data between tenants).
- The provisioned instance's resource requests/limits match the benchmark-informed sizing
  recommendation.
- Lifecycle behaviors are explicitly designed and tested: the instance is cleaned up when its
  consuming playground is deleted, recovers after pod restarts, and credentials can be rotated
  without manual intervention.
- The PostgreSQL image used is the existing Red Hat image with pgvector included; no custom image

- The BFF can be repointed at a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL connection string without
  rearchitecting the provisioning (portability verified by design review or configuration test).
- Disabling the default provisioning and configuring an external vector database instead is
  supported and documented.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-1 (P0) — default vector store out-of-the-box:** this epic is the BFF-managed delivery of
  that capability.
- **HLR-2 (P0) — playground RAG with no loss of current capability:** covered by the end-to-end
  validation acceptance criteria (Gen AI Studio only; Auto Rag decoupled per Staff input).
- **HLR-3 (P0) — separate-process, non-inline vector store:** delivered via the remote pgvector
  vector_io provider configuration on the OGXServer custom resource.
- **HLR-4 (P1) — multi-tenant scoping (bundled):** implements the scoping model resolved by the
  scoping investigation; enforcing it is the same provisioning code and resource surface as HLR-1, so
  it is not split into a separate epic.
- **HLR-5 (P1) — lightweight/overhead (bundled):** applies the benchmark-informed resource sizing to

- **HLR-6 (P2) — portability to a platform-shared database (bundled):** the connection-string

  this branch epic exists at all; the failure impact above covers the scoping gate.

# Determine the scoping model for the Gen AI Studio default vector store

## Description

This investigation resolves the strategy's open question of how the default pgvector-backed vector
store for Gen AI Studio playground RAG is scoped: per namespace, per OGX server instance, or both.
The Gen AI Studio lead prefers per-namespace for isolation, but the original per-instance motivation
(Auto Rag) has been moved out of this strategy's scope. The answer determines the provisioning
topology — which Kubernetes resources are shared versus per-scope — that the downstream provisioning
implementation builds, so it must be resolved before that implementation is finalized.

## Scope

- Analyze the OGXServer custom resource topology and the gen-ai BFF's playground/OGXServer creation
  path to enumerate what each scoping model implies concretely (shared vs per-scope PostgreSQL
  deployments, services, persistent volume claims, and credentials).
- Evaluate multi-tenant isolation under each model: data visibility across namespaces and across
  playgrounds sharing a scope, and blast radius of instance failure.
- Evaluate resource overhead of each model against the strategy's requirement that the default store
  be lightweight in resource-constrained environments.
- Recommend one scoping model (per namespace, per instance, or both, with a stated rule for when each
  applies), with the recommendation stated precisely enough to be implemented and tested.
- Identify any consequence for the connection configuration handed to the OGX vector_io provider.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A written decision records the selected scoping model (per namespace, per OGX server instance, or
  both) with rationale covering multi-tenant isolation, coupling to OGX instances, and resource
  overhead, and is accepted by the Gen AI Studio team.
- The decision enumerates the concrete provisioning topology it implies — which Kubernetes resources

# Benchmark pgvector against the inline Milvus baseline and recommend resource sizing

## Description

This epic delivers the sprint-1 benchmark the Staff Engineer Input calls for: capture the inline
Milvus performance baseline used by Gen AI Studio playground RAG today, verify that pgvector (with
flat scan, no index) is in the same order of magnitude for typical playground workloads, and produce
a resource sizing recommendation for the default pgvector instance starting from the
model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits. The default store targets development
experimentation, not production: strict latency SLAs are explicitly out of scope, and users with
production-scale vector workloads are directed to an external vector database.

## Scope

- Capture baseline metrics for representative playground RAG operations (document ingest and
  retrieval over small document sets) against the current inline Milvus provider.
- Run the same representative workload against a PostgreSQL instance with the pgvector extension
  using flat scan (no vector index), matching the intended default configuration.
- Record latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) for both as informational data — the pass condition is
  order-of-magnitude equivalence, not a threshold.
- Produce a resource sizing recommendation (CPU/memory requests and limits, storage) for the default
  pgvector instance, starting from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing and adjusted based
  on the benchmark observations.
- Document the scope limits of the default store in the benchmark report: development-experimentation
  target, flat scan, small document sets, and the recommendation that production-scale workloads use
  an external vector database.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Inline Milvus baseline metrics for the representative playground RAG workload are captured and
  recorded in the benchmark report.
- pgvector results for the same workload are recorded, and the report states whether pgvector is
  within the same order of magnitude as the inline Milvus baseline.
- A resource sizing recommendation (requests/limits/storage) is produced, starting from the
  model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing and adjusted per the benchmark observations, in a form
  the provisioning implementation can apply directly.
- The report documents the scope limits: no latency SLA, flat scan (no index), small document sets,
  and external vector database recommended for production-scale workloads.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-5 (P1) — default store lightweight enough for resource-constrained environments without
  significant overhead:** this epic delivers the order-of-magnitude comparison and the sizing
  recommendation that verify the requirement. The provisioning implementation applies the
  recommended sizing as part of its own deliverable (bundled there — applying the limits is an edit to
  the same provisioned Deployment spec, so it is not split into a separate epic).
